St. Peter's Basilica. The largest church in the world and the spiritual center of the Roman Catholic Church, built over more than a century—from 1506 to 1626—to replace an ancient church on this same site in Rome.

Pope Julius II commissioned the basilica in 1506 to honor Saint Peter, whose burial on this ground was believed to form the basis of papal authority. The construction was overseen by a succession of architectural geniuses: Donato Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo, and Carlo Maderno. Michelangelo, who designed the iconic dome, famously donated his own labor out of piety.

That dome stands 136 meters tall and remains one of the most recognized architectural forms in the world, dominating Rome's skyline even today. Archaeological excavations have uncovered a necropolis beneath the altar, lending historical weight to the sanctity of the site.

Funding for the construction came partly through the sale of indulgences—a practice that would spark Martin Luther's critique and the Protestant Reformation itself. Pope Leo X particularly funded construction through indulgence preacher Johann Tetzel's aggressive campaigns in Northern Europe.

The baroque master Gian Lorenzo Bernini transformed the basilica's interior and exterior. He designed the grand colonnade piazza surrounding the church, the magnificent baldachin, or canopy, over the high altar, and numerous sculptures that exemplify the grandeur of the Counter-Reformation. The basilica contains over a hundred chapels and abundant masterpieces by artists like Raphael and Caravaggio, along with the tombs of popes including Peter himself.

The 120-year construction process revealed the tensions between Renaissance idealism and baroque drama. Wars, financial crises, and changing architectural visions all contributed to the prolonged timeline. Yet this very length made St. Peter's simultaneously Christendom's greatest architectural achievement and, through its funding, an unwitting catalyst for Christianity's greatest schism.

Vatican City is the sovereign city-state where St. Peter's Basilica stands as the seat of papal authority. The Counter-Reformation, the Church's artistic and spiritual response to the Reformation, is magnificently expressed throughout the basilica's baroque decoration.
